entities.name: Achille Liénart
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Achille Liénart (1884–1973) was a French cardinal and Bishop of Lille who became internationally known for a single decisive intervention at the opening of the Second Vatican Council in October 1962. Ordained in 1907, he became Bishop of Lille in 1928 and was elevated to cardinal in 1930, serving the industrial diocese of northern France through the Depression, World War II occupation, and postwar reconstruction.

At the first working session of Vatican II on 13 October 1962, Liénart dramatically interrupted the scheduled vote on commission memberships—which would have preserved curial dominance—to demand more time for bishops to consult one another. His intervention, immediately seconded by Cardinal Josef Frings of Cologne, broke the pre-arranged curial script and set the council on a more collegial, reform-oriented course. It was widely regarded as the moment the council found its independent voice, freeing the assembled bishops from automatic deference to Roman preparatory commissions.

As Bishop of Lille he was also known for his support of the worker-priest movement and his engagement with the social questions of an industrial diocese. His social concern informed his conciliar activism: he believed the Church needed to speak credibly to modern industrial society, which required internal renewal. Liénart died in 1973, having witnessed the implementation of the council he helped shape.
